articles.title: Minnesota GOP chair blasts progressive group over KKK-themed sign shown during Black House speaker's remarks
articles.summary: Sunrise Movement Twin Cities said it disrupted a Minnesota Republican Party fundraiser, displaying a "RepubliKKKan Party" banner during Lisa Demuth's remarks.
articles.body: Minnesota's Republican Party chairman is accusing protesters of racial intimidation after demonstrators disrupted a GOP dinner and displayed a sign invoking the Ku Klux Klan while the state's first Black female House speaker addressed the crowd. Minnesota GOP Chair Alex Plechash blasted the demonstrators in a statement after Friday night's Lincoln Reagan Dinner in Eagan, where protesters held a sign reading "RepubliKKKan Party" during remarks by House Speaker and Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth. "Last night, radical protesters stormed the stage at our Lincoln Reagan Dinner and held up a KKK symbol while Speaker Lisa Demuth spoke," Plechash said in a statement posted to X by the Republican Party of Minnesota. DAVID MARCUS: MINNESOTA GOP CANDIDATES KEEP TRUMP AT ARM'S LENGTH AS THEY EYE A POST-TRUMP PARTY FUTURE "Let's be clear about what happened. Left leaning protesters aimed a symbol of racial terror at a Black woman leader, at a dinner named for the president who ended slavery," he continued. Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, a progressive activist organization, claimed responsibility for the disruption and said the demonstration was intended to protest Republican policies it believes harm immigrants and marginalized communities, according to local news station KTSP. "We disrupted this fundraiser because we refuse to give a moment's peace to the people bankrolling racial violence," the group said in a statement cited by the outlet. The organization also said it was not affiliated with Minnesota's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL). Video of the incident shows demonstrators moving toward the front of the room holding signs, including one with the letters "KKK" highlighted in red, according to outlet. One protester could be heard shouting, "You love Trump and you will not stand up for Minnesotans," as Demuth stood on stage holding a microphone. As security escorted the demonstrators away, attendees began chanting, "Lisa," followed by chants of, "USA." Plechash told the outlet that protesters gained access to the dinner by purchasing tickets and passing through security checkpoints. KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?' The chairman said the event experienced two disruptions, the first during remarks by Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya and the second while Demuth was speaking. Plechash said roughly three or four protesters pushed toward the front of the room carrying banners during Demuth's remarks. He estimated the disruption lasted about 30 seconds and said he did not believe the demonstrators posed a physical threat. Plechash said in his X post that Eagan police issued trespass orders and that potential charges remained under investigation. The GOP chairman also called out Minnesota Democrats, specifically naming the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. "Intimidation, criminal behavior, and racist rhetoric have no place in Minnesota politics," Plechash wrote. "Republicans debate ideas, and we'd welcome the DFL to show up and do the same," he added. "Every hour they stay silent says something. Their silence is deafening." Tim Walz.

articles.title: Sen. Thom Tillis says he believes Trump’s fuel deal with Russia could be breaking the law
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia in order to allow Russia to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.
articles.body: Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia to allow it to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law. “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said. Trump announced in a Friday post on Truth Social that Russia would “immediately supply” hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global marketplace, with more than 1 million additional tons soon on the way. The move drew sharp condemnation from Ukraine and critics of the Trump administration. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, lawmakers took a series of steps to try to financially punish the Kremlin. In 2022, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to ban Russian oil imports, and Congress has not made changes to the law to reflect the president’s announcement. Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he believes the president is breaking the law with his Russia deal, Tillis said, “I believe that he may be.” “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor,” he added. “Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied.” The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the senator’s remarks. Tillis referenced year-end congressional funding negotiations when asked what the Senate could do if Tillis believes Trump is breaking the law. “If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” he said. Asked whether Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin was putting American lives at risk, Tillis said, “It absolutely will,” pointing to Russian funding of mercenaries and the Kremlin’s relationship with Iran. Tillis has just months remaining before his term expires. His retirement from the Senate created a high-profile battleground opening. Democrats are eyeing his seat as a prime target to flip as they seek control of the chamber. Tillis has been highly critical of aspects of the Trump administration, including the performance of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Tillis, who voted for Hegseth’s confirmation, now says he regrets his vote. Tillis on Sunday condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 mass shooting in Fort Hood, Texas. Tillis said that the livestream plans would radicalize people and be used by terrorist groups as a recruiting tool. “The Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life,” he said. “This is not who we are, and it’s another example of why Pete Hegseth, in all of his bravado, needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader, and we need strong leadership supporting President Trump right now,” he added.

articles.title: Guilfoyle told Greek businessman ‘I’m going to make you a lot of f—ing money’: Report
articles.summary: The Trump administration is reportedly weighing whether to remove U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle from her role as new allegations emerge that wealthy Greek businessmen paid for her luxury travel while she used her diplomatic position to lobby their business interests. According to a new report from the Wall Street Journal, senior Trump administration…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is reportedly weighing whether to remove U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle from her role as new allegations emerge that wealthy Greek businessmen paid for her luxury travel while she used her diplomatic position to lobby their business interests.

According to a new report from the Wall Street Journal, senior Trump administration officials are discussing Guilfoyle’s future and a decision from President Trump is expected soon.

During January’s World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Guilfoyle allegedly boasted about her connections to the wealthy businessmen while trying to secure an invitation from an American businessman to a dinner honoring the president’s son, Eric Trump, according to an audio recording reviewed by the Journal.

“You know, I can deliver the world to you. Which you deserve,” Guilfoyle told the American businessman in the audio. “I’m going to make you a lot of f—ing money.”

The State Department’s inspector general is also investigating whether the ambassador accepted gifts or favors from private businessmen, according to the Journal, who cited a person familiar with the matter.

The Hill has reached out to the White House and the State Department for comment.

The government watchdog’s probe comes after former attorney and longtime Trump ally Eric Deters accused her of requesting $100,000 from him to clear her American Express credit card bill days before her confirmation hearing last year in exchange for lobbying top administration officials on his behalf.

The latest scrutiny centers on Guilfoyle’s relationships with two prominent Greek business tycoons who reportedly provided her with private jet travel and other luxury accommodations.

Guilfoyle, who was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and was the ex-fiancé of Donald Trump Jr., also spoke about flying to Davos on a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, CEO of Greek construction company Aktor Group. The Journal previously reported that she had encouraged governments across southeastern Europe to purchase billions of dollars in American natural gas through Exarchou’s company.

She also described plans to travel to Paris with Greek shipping mogul Nikolas Tsakos, who later paid for her stay at the luxurious Four Seasons Hotel George V, the Journal reported.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Athens defended Guilfoyle in a statement to the Journal, saying she had “faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines.”

articles.title: Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
articles.summary: Trump has long criticised US military support for Ukraine and has lambasted Zelenskyy since his first term.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has called for the removal of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after blaming the Ukrainian leader for rising diesel prices, which have put pressure on the Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections.

The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have increased after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.

“I think it’s ⁠⁠⁠⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.

“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump added.

Zelenskyy on Sunday pushed back, vowing to continue striking Russian oil refineries. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.

“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so,” he said.

This is not the first time Trump has lambasted Zelenskyy. Their tense relationship goes back to Trump’s first term as president, when he pressured Zelenskyy to investigate his rival, Joe Biden, and his son, Hunter Biden.

Here’s a timeline of some of the occasions when Trump has been critical of Zelenskyy:

October 2026: In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.

“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t ‌‌‌‌hit ‌‌‌‌refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.

Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.

The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries.

Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished, he added.

April 2025: On April 15 , Trump criticised Zelenskyy and implied Kyiv had started the war against Russia, saying the Ukrainian leader was “always looking to purchase” US missiles. “You don’t start a war against someone 20 times your size and hope people give you some missiles,” Trump said.

Then on April 23 , he criticised Zelenskyy for making “very harmful” statements after the Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea of ceding occupied Crimea to Russia in a potential peace deal.

Zelenskyy had ruled out ceding any territory, declaring, “There is nothing to talk about – it is our land, the land of the Ukrainian people”.

In a post on his social media platform, Trump accused Zelenskyy of stoking tension by “boasting” that Kyiv would not legally recognise ceding Crimea to Russia.

“This statement is very harmful to the Peace Negotiations with Russia,” Trump said, adding that Russia invaded the Crimean Peninsula and annexed it back in 2014 “without a shot being fired”.

“It’s inflammatory statements like Zelenskyy’s that makes it so difficult to settle this War,” Trump said. “He can have Peace or, he can fight for another three years before losing the whole Country.”

Despite the tension, the two leaders held a private meeting at the Vatican on April 26, 2025, during Pope Francis’s funeral.

Feb 28, 2025: During their fiery Oval Office meeting, Trump and Vice President JD Vance clashed with Zelenskyy over rare earth mineral agreements, security assurances and peace negotiations with Russia.

Trump warned Zelenskyy, “You’re either going to make a deal [on ending the war with Russia] or we’re out,” and accused the Ukrainian leader of having “disrespected” the United States and “overplayed his hand”.

The US president and Vance also berated Zelenskyy for lacking gratitude and refusing to compromise to end the war, with Trump arguing that Zelenskyy was unready for peace.

The meeting devolved into a shouting match and Zelenskyy departed the White House abruptly.

February 19, 2025: A month after returning to power for a second term, Trump called the Ukrainian president a “dictator without elections” and accused him of wanting to keep the “gravy train” of US military support going while Washington tries to end the war with Russia.

In a lengthy and scathing post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump accused Zelenskyy of taking US money and embroiling the country in an endless conflict.

He later doubled down on those comments, telling an audience at an investment summit in Miami that Zelenskyy had “done a terrible job, his country is shattered, and millions and millions of people have unnecessarily died”.

“A dictator without elections. Zelenskyy better move fast or he’s not going to have a country left. Gotta move. Gotta move fast cause that war’s going in the wrong direction,” Trump said on stage at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute summit.

“In the meantime, we’re successfully negotiating an end to the war with Russia. Something I’ll admit that only Trump is going to be able to do and the Trump administration – we’re going to be able to do it. I think Putin even admitted that,” he said.

“Biden never tried. Europe has failed to bring peace and Zelenskyy probably wants to, maybe he wants to keep the gravy train going. I don’t know what’s the problem, but he has been able. He’s very upset,” he added.

Trump had been critical of Biden’s financial and military support to Ukraine during the war. He had vowed to end the war within 24 hours of his taking office, but later said he was being “sarcastic”.

2024 Campaign trail: On the 2024 US presidential election campaign trail, Trump repeatedly criticised Zelenskyy for not trying hard enough to end Russia’s war on Ukraine. In September, at an election rally speech in North Carolina, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy for refusing to negotiate, stating that even the “worst deal” or giving up a small amount of territory would be better than ongoing death and destruction.

July 2019: During his first term, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to work with Rudy Giuliani and the US attorney general to investigate Democratic political rival Joe Biden. That is according to a five-page memo summarising the July 25 call.

At the time of the call, the Trump administration was also withholding from Ukraine nearly $400m in congressionally approved security assistance, prompting speculation the US president was using the money as leverage to get his desired investigations.

Zelenskyy expressed willingness to look into new cases and cooperate with US investigations, though he and Ukrainian officials later maintained they did not feel directly threatened or pressured during the conversation itself.

articles.title: Trump announces immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine
articles.summary: President Donald Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire, but his recent deal easing Russian diesel exports drew sharp criticism from Kyiv.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, saying both countries have agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure after weeks of escalating tensions over strikes on oil refineries and power plants. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. The announcement comes as Trump has intensified pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, arguing that the attacks have disrupted global diesel supplies and contributed to higher fuel prices for American consumers. The issue has become increasingly urgent as diesel prices weigh on American farmers, truckers and businesses that rely on the fuel to transport goods and operate heavy equipment. RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS MIDTERMS LOOM AND WAR IN UKRAINE AND IRAN WAGES ON Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, even as Kyiv maintains that targeting Moscow's oil industry is a legitimate strategy to weaken Russia's ability to finance its war. The announcement follows a contentious week in U.S.-Ukraine relations after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel exports to reach American and global markets. Under the agreement announced Friday, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, with additional shipments expected in November and beyond. The Treasury Department also authorized temporary sanctions relief to facilitate Russian diesel supplies. Trump argued that the agreement would help bring down fuel prices, while Zelenskyy criticized the decision as a concession to Moscow that could provide additional revenue for Russia's war effort. The dispute escalated Saturday when Trump suggested Ukraine should replace Zelenskyy with a leader more willing to negotiate an end to the war. "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," Trump told reporters. 'OUR POSITION IS CLEAR:' ZELENSKYY AND EU DISMISS CEDING UKRAINIAN LAND TO RUSSIA Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has maintained that Ukraine would be willing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to stop targeting Ukrainian power plants and other critical infrastructure. The two countries have increasingly targeted each other's energy systems throughout the war, although the consequences have differed. Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid have left civilians facing electricity disruptions and damaged infrastructure needed to heat homes and sustain businesses. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, meanwhile, have disrupted fuel production and exports, putting additional pressure on global energy markets. The Trump administration has spent weeks attempting to negotiate a reciprocal halt to energy attacks as part of broader diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the war. In September, Trump similarly announced that both countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, although Moscow did not publicly confirm the agreement and attacks continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest announcement raises the possibility of renewed diplomatic progress, but an energy ceasefire would not amount to a comprehensive agreement to end the fighting. It was not immediately clear how the agreement would be monitored or enforced. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fox News Digital reached out to the Ukrainian and Russian embassies in Washington, D.C., seeking confirmation of the ceasefire but did not immediately receive responses.

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time could leave students commuting in the dark, data shows
articles.summary: While permanent daylight saving time would cause the sun to set later in winter, the sun would, in turn, rise later in the morning.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Nineteen states and those who wish our clocks didn’t “fall back” in November may have seen the light at the end of the tunnel after the House passed a President Trump-backed bill to make daylight saving time permanent earlier this year.

Any hopes of being able to leave the clocks as they are in the early hours of November may have only been dashed after the Senate adjourned without taking any action on the Sunshine Protection Act.

Some anger may have been passed off to Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas), who has frequently spoken out against the bill, after President Trump shared his cellphone number online and told people to tell Cotton “it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN.”

Cotton, however, responded by reiterating his stance that “no one likes changing the clock, me included,” while pointing to previous less-than-successful efforts by the U.S. to observe permanent daylight saving time.

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” Cotton wrote on X .

But just how dark would it be when your kids head off to school? It depends on where you live.

Generally speaking, in the U.S., most to all sunrises from early November to early-to-mid March — the time in which we observe standard time currently — happen somewhere in the 6 or 7 o’clock hours . There are outliers, especially further north. In Lansing, Michigan, for example, more than 40 of the 133 sunrises between the clocks changing will happen after 8 a.m.

If we, instead, observed daylight saving time year-round, those sunrises would shift an hour later. Lansing would see 129 sunrises after 8 a.m., and 43 would happen after 9 a.m.

Your child, of course, doesn’t have to go to school all of the 133 days between our clocks falling back to standard time and springing forward to daylight saving time. So how many days would they actually be commuting “in the pitch dark?”

When would your kids commute in the dark?

Let’s say, for example, your child has to leave for school at 7 a.m. We’ll also assume your child has 85 days of school between the clocks changing in November and March, removing weekends and major holidays (Thanksgiving and Black Friday, plus the several days from Christmas Eve to the first Monday after New Year’s Day) from the tally above.

Nexstar tallied the sunrise times for 62 U.S. cities across the 85 typical school days between November and March.

At present, on average, a child matching the above example leaves for school before the sun rises about 50 times. The other 35 days, the sun comes up before the child leaves at 7 a.m.

If we began observing year-round daylight saving time, only two cities would have at least two school day sunrises before 7 a.m.: Las Vegas (two) and Panama City, Florida (six). In other communities, several sunrises wouldn’t happen until after 8 a.m., Nexstar found.

The interactive table below shows how many sunrises happen before 7 a.m. on traditional school days now. Since only two cities analyzed would see any sunrises before 7 a.m., the second column shows how many school-day sunrises would happen after 8 a.m. if daylight saving time became permanent.

There are limitations and caveats to the data above. It doesn’t take into account additional days off your child may have, for example, or if they have to leave home before or after 7 a.m.

Regardless, history may be on Cotton’s side.

The U.S. briefly observed permanent daylight saving time in 1973 ( among other times in the 1900s ). It was highly regarded at first, with a nearly 80% approval rate in December of that year, The New York Times reported. Two months later, that had dropped to 42%.

The discontent, at least in part, appeared to be fueled by parents sending their children to school in the dark, armed with flashlights and prompting safety concerns. There were multiple incidents nationwide of children being struck by vehicles while on their way to school, including eight fatalities in Florida . The U.S. would return to seasonal clock changes by fall of 1974.

The U.S. Department of Transportation, meanwhile, found no clear evidence regarding traffic accidents in relation to year-round daylight saving time. It also determined that energy savings, another purported benefit of locking the clocks that Trump has touted , were a meager 0.4% to 1.5%.

It’s difficult to say. The Senate could take up the Sunshine Protection Act when they return in mid-November, though Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) recently said there is “no clear path forward” for the legislation. Plus, the current Congress is only expected to remain in session through about mid- to late December.

Congress is also considering two bills in the House that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, a bill to make half-daylight saving time permanent and a newly introduced bill to make standard time permanent , with exceptions.

For now, though, our clocks appear likely to “fall back” to standard time in the early morning hours of Nov. 1.

articles.title: Honor the Rosies where they belong: On the National Mall
articles.summary: Each year, there are fewer living Rosies. Those of us left hope to see firsthand the day that our efforts, and our sacrifices, are remembered and honored on the National Mall alongside our memorials commemorating America’s heroes.
articles.body:
I was 17 years old when I first picked up a rivet gun.

It was the summer of 1943, and I had started my first-ever job attaching sheet metal to the frames of airplane wings — mostly B-17s and B-29s, U.S. military aircraft used during the Second World War. The job paid well, but what I remember most is how proud I was to be contributing to the war effort, to something bigger and more important than myself.

Though I didn’t know it at the time, my decision that summer to leave my small North Dakota hometown for Seattle to join The Boeing Co. marked my initiation into an incredible contingent of women with bandanas and can-do attitudes who would one day become American icons.

The “Rosie the Riveters,” or more simply the “Rosies,” are the 18 million American women who answered the call when legions of men across the United States departed to fight the Axis powers. We worked long hours carefully assembling the planes, tanks and ships that would be sent to support the war overseas. But women served in many other roles, keeping America’s entire economic engine running.

They were mechanics, pilots, engineers, electricians, code breakers, autoworkers, lumberjacks, farmers and ranchers — united in their effort to hold down the home front. These often overlooked jobs demonstrated the wide range of responsibilities women took on during the war, helping to reshape perceptions of what women could contribute both in the workforce and in national service.

We didn’t do the work for praise but to save our country and our family members who were overseas. We felt the call to serve just as strongly as the men did. And the women of the Greatest Generation helped secure Allied victory, saved American lives, and strengthened the home front during one of the most consequential periods in our history.

As we celebrate America250 this year, it is a unique opportunity to recognize the Rosies as enduring symbols of civic pride, sacrifice and devotion to the American ideal. The strength of our nation has always depended on ordinary citizens willing to do extraordinary things in service to their country. The Rosies were no exception, embodying the American tradition of service every day they dutifully showed up to work.

In 2024, I was asked to accept the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of these 18 million women. It was the honor of my lifetime. A memorial on the National Mall would ensure that honor endures for generations to come.

Recognizing the Rosies’ lasting impact on the U.S., Congress passed bipartisan legislation in 2022 authorizing a national memorial to the women who served on the home front during World War II. This memorial will not only honor their service but also educate future generations about the indispensable role women played in securing victory and advancing the cause of freedom.

The effort is now in the site selection and approval phase. And I believe the National Mall, in close proximity to the existing World War II Memorial, is the most fitting and prominent location for telling this important chapter of American history.

There is bipartisan legislation in Congress that would allow just that. The World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act would permit the memorial to be located on or near the National Mall, placing the story of America’s World War II women alongside the memorial honoring the esteemed veterans who fought overseas. Late last year, the House of Representatives passed the World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act with overwhelming bipartisan support. However, the bill is now stalled in the Senate.

I refuse to let that be the end of our story.

Each year, there are fewer living Rosies. Those of us left hope to see firsthand the day that our efforts, and our sacrifices, are remembered and honored on the National Mall alongside our memorials commemorating America’s heroes.

This year, I turned 100 years old. But I remain as determined as I was at 17 when I left home to pick up a rivet gun. So I am calling on the Senate to pass — and President Trump to sign — the World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act. We answered our country’s call when freedom was at stake. Now, I ask our nation to ensure that our story, and the lessons it carries, will never be forgotten.

Mae Krier is an original Rosie the Riveter who worked on Boeing aircraft during World War II, from 1943 to 1945. She helped to establish National Rosie the Riveter Day in 2017 and accepted the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of all her fellow Rosies in 2024.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to ‘energy ceasefire’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he was unaware of the deal, but that Ukraine would back it.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has announced what he called an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Ukraine and Russia, after mutual attacks on energy infrastructure piled pressure on global energy prices.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed,” Trump wrote on social media on Sunday. “Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios.

But he confirmed Ukraine would back the deal, saying in a post on Telegram: “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side.”

Zelenskyy previously said on Sunday he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day full ceasefire.

On Saturday, Trump slammed the Ukrainian president for attacking Russian oil refineries, the day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were originally imposed to sap Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.

“He better damn well stop,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added.

Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.

“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.

“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”

The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment , with attacks intensifying in the past few months.

On Saturday, a six-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled her from the wreckage.

In response to Trump’s suggestion of a new leader, Zelenskyy said, “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.body:
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) paid a Kansas bakery $1,300 Saturday after its owner publicly accused his campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years.

The payment came days after Holly Thomas, owner of Holly’s Sweet Treats in Hutchinson, Kan., said Marshall’s 2020 Senate campaign never paid for cookies, cupcakes and brownies ordered for his Republican primary election watch party.

Marshall said he had no knowledge of the outstanding bill and moved to settle it after learning of Thomas’s claims.

“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double,” Marshall wrote on social media Saturday.

The senator also shared a screenshot of a digital receipt showing a $1,300 payment to the bakery.

Thomas said Thursday that the campaign had left her with a $678.75 bill at a time when her newly opened business was struggling through the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Do you know why I will never vote for Roger Marshall?” Thomas wrote on Facebook . “Because six years ago, when I was a brand-new small business owner, his campaign ordered cookies and treats from my bakery for his primary election watch party. And I never got paid.”

According to an invoice Thomas shared, the campaign ordered $375 worth of custom sugar cookies, $75 in cupcakes and $175 in fudge brownies.

Thomas said she spent nearly a year trying to collect payment, repeatedly contacting the campaign by phone and email without receiving a response.

“Not only was I just starting out, but we were also in the middle of COVID, when small businesses everywhere were struggling just to keep their doors open. Every single dollar mattered,” she wrote. “Those cookies and treats cost money to make, employees’ time to prepare, and resources that my little business couldn’t afford to give away.”

Marshall, a physician who was first elected to the Senate in 2020, has previously been scrutinized over his medical practice’s efforts to collect unpaid bills from patients. The New York Times uncovered hundreds of debt collection lawsuits involving the practice.

articles.title: Trump, Vance blitz Ohio as Democrats look to flip governor’s mansion
articles.summary: The red-leaning Buckeye State governor’s mansion could flip for the first time in two decades as Democrat Amy Acton narrowly leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in recent polls of their bitter midterm battle. A new CNN poll Thursday showed Acton up 8 percentage points over Ramaswamy, after a New York Times/Siena poll found Acton ahead by…
articles.body:
The red-leaning Buckeye State governor’s mansion could flip for the first time in two decades as Democrat Amy Acton narrowly leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in recent polls of their bitter midterm battle.

A new CNN poll Thursday showed Acton up 8 percentage points over Ramaswamy, after a New York Times/Siena poll found Acton ahead by 4 points last week. Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages now show Acton up roughly 4 points, rating the race a toss-up.

The wide-open race to succeed outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine (R) comes against the backdrop of a highly competitive Senate race and a handful of battleground House contests, putting Republicans on defense in races they’ve easily won in recent years.

Ohio is the latest red stronghold in the spotlight of President Trump’s cross-country campaign blitz as he seeks to energize base voters. After Trump rallied outside Dayton for Ramaswamy last weekend, Vice President Vance stopped in Lima on Friday and Trump is headed to Youngstown on Monday to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

“I think Republicans are clearly very concerned about Ohio,” said Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

“There are a set of races that they probably expected to be safer, and they are seeing a few of those races, if not slip away, then certainly look more precarious for them, and you can see that by where Trump and Vance are going.”

Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur who ran for president in 2024, boasts prime endorsements from DeWine, Vance and Trump in his bid for a governor’s mansion that Republicans have held since 2010.

He was a controversial candidate but effusive ally of Trump even as they fought for the GOP’s White House nod last cycle and was later tapped to help lead Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) crackdown on federal spending alongside tech mogul Elon Musk. And with a net worth estimated at $2.3 billion, Ramaswamy has been able to partially self-fund his midterm bid at home in Ohio.

But Republicans across the country face significant midterm headwinds — from Trump’s sunken approval ratings to the historic trend of the ruling party losing out between presidential cycles — and Ramaswamy faces tough competition in Acton.

A physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton worked with DeWine and other Republican leaders as she led the state’s response to the pandemic. Supporters have touted her bipartisan work along the campaign trail, arguing Acton “ will work with anyone .” Like Ramaswamy, she has not held elected office before.

“The governor’s race is very unusual because we have unusual candidates for each party … neither of them are really conventional candidates,” Buchler said.

And with less than a month to go until Election Day, the rivals have been ramping up their attacks.

Acton’s campaign has painted Ramaswamy as an out-of-touch billionaire, while Republican groups have accused Acton of being an alcoholic and drug addict — claims she’s decried as “horrible.” There is currently no scheduled debate between the two candidates.

Meanwhile, the Senate race between Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is also considered a critical toss-up in the fight for control of the upper chamber.

Brown led by 6 points in the CNN polling and by 4 points in The New York Times results, while Husted led by 1 point in a co/efficient survey.

Acton’s campaign manager, Philip Stein, said the numbers are a signal that “Ohioans are ready for a change.”

But Republicans in the state are shaking off the polls and pointing to their past winning streak.

“It’s a Republican state and more red in midterm elections, and that serves Vivek Ramaswamy and John Husted and the Republicans up and down the ticket well,” said Ohio GOP consultant Matt Dole.

“It’s certainly closer — you know, our governor won by 27 points or something like that four years ago — it’s not that type of environment, and certainly the national environment is challenging,” Dole said. “But I think the fundamentals still, despite what the polls say, are advantageous for Republicans.”

Others say a red win is more uncertain as Trump’s approval declines among voters in Ohio, a state where Republicans easily outnumber Democrats.

Robert Alexander, a political science professor at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, said that the tight polls, the ad blitz and “multiple visits from Trump and Vance” signal that “those polls probably aren’t too far off, and that they also expect a very close race.”

Trump “is not what he was certainly two years ago,” Alexander said, which might mean a “backlash effect” from disaffected Republicans or independents frustrated by the status quo.

“The Democrat brand is not as strong in the state as the Republican brand … but the headwinds against Republicans right now are pretty strong.”

After casting his own early ballot Friday in Ohio, Vance urged the crowd in Lima to vote for both Husted and Ramaswamy — saying Republicans “need” Ramaswamy to win “because he is running against a crazy person.” The vice president was notably a senator for Ohio for just two years before he was tapped to join Trump’s presidential ticket.

In Vandalia, Ohio, last weekend, Trump urged supporters to turn out and vote red no matter what.

“Go out and vote. Even if you hate Jon Husted, even if you hate Vivek Ramaswamy, you’re gonna go out, you’re gonna vote, and then you’re gonna pull their triggers,” Trump said.

Amid Trump’s poor approval rating, Ohio Democratic strategist Jeff Rusnak suggested the president’s trip could backfire.

“I think what he’s doing is firing up Democrats and Independents who are really turned off by him and even some of those Republicans who have had enough,” Rusnak said, arguing Trump is “in for a rude awakening” when he talks to voters in the Mahoning Valley on Monday.

But observers on all sides of the aisle agree the Senate and gubernatorial races will come down to turnout, as evidenced by Trump’s call to Ohioans with early and absentee voting already underway .

“Preferences, I think, are leaning toward Democrats in the state this year, but those preferences don’t translate to votes,” Alexander said.

He described a “nightmare scenario” for Republicans in which some voters don’t want Acton or Brown on the Democratic side — but still aren’t “excited” enough about Ramaswamy or Husted in the GOP column.

“It’s cliche to say it all depends on turnout, but that’s the reality, and I think that’s exactly why you’re seeing Trump and Vance come to the state.”

articles.title: WATCH: CDC director discusses US government response to Russian plague concerns: 'We are protected'
articles.summary: CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz says the agency is monitoring travelers from Siberia amid concerns about a pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia.
articles.body: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is coordinating with federal agencies to monitor travelers entering the United States from Siberia amid concerns about a possible pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia, the agency's director revealed Wednesday. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said the Trump administration is working across multiple agencies to identify travelers arriving from the region following the mysterious death of a Russian laboratory worker, while emphasizing that the risk to Americans remains minimal. "We are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low," Schwartz said during a Wall Street Journal health forum Wednesday. MOTHER OF DEAD RUSSIAN ANTI-PLAGUE INSTITUTE WORKER: 'I KNOW THE TRUTH' The concerns stem from the Oct. 2 death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, whose death has fueled speculation about a possible pneumonic plague infection. Russian authorities have maintained that Shipilova died from pneumonia of unknown origin and have not confirmed that she was infected with Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes pneumonic plague. Schwartz said the CDC is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State and War, among other federal agencies, to track potential arrivals from the region. "There are about 200 flights that come into the United States from Siberia, that region," Schwartz said, adding that those flights typically arrive at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. "We have a port health station set up in JFK so that we can do appropriate surveillance and screening if anyone from that area comes into the United States," she continued. The CDC director stressed that while pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection capable of spreading between people through respiratory droplets, early detection and treatment can prevent deaths. TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP' "The one good thing, if I could say there's a good thing, is that it's a treatable, highly treatable bacterial disease with common antibiotics that most physicians within the United States can utilize," Schwartz said. The illness is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is considered the most serious form of plague, according to the CDC. Symptoms can include fever, chest pain, coughing and rapidly developing pneumonia. Without prompt antibiotic treatment, the infection can be fatal, the agency warns. The World Health Organization (WHO) has pressed Moscow for additional information about Shipilova's death. Russian authorities placed approximately 200 people who had contact with the deceased laboratory worker under quarantine, according to Euronews. On Thursday, Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said preventive measures had been completed and roughly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no pathogens, according to the Associated Press. RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP However, Russian officials have not publicly identified the pathogen responsible for Shipilova's pneumonia or definitively ruled out pneumonic plague as the cause of her death, according to The Associated Press. Asked whether Moscow was being sufficiently transparent with American authorities, Schwartz indicated that the administration was still seeking answers. "We are still having those conversations about what exactly happened in Siberia," she said, adding that U.S. officials were working with information about an unconfirmed case of pneumonic plague.

articles.title: Rescue expert warns FlyDubai hijacking attempt shows US, allies are ‘playing checkers’ against terror threat
articles.summary: Bryan Stern, a 9/11 first responder and rescue expert, warns the FlyDubai hijacking exposes how far behind Western counterterrorism strategy has fallen.
articles.body: The FlyDubai attempted hijacking shows the U.S. and its allies are still using outdated counterterrorism assumptions against increasingly sophisticated enemies, a U.S. rescue expert and 9/11 first responder warns. "They’re good at chess," Bryan Stern, chairman and CEO of Grey Bull Rescue, told Fox News Digital on Monday, saying the radical ideology behind the FlyDubai attack is a ringing "bell" for global aviation security and Western counterterrorism strategy. "And we’re, if we’re lucky, playing checkers – if we’re lucky – and I would argue we’re not even playing checkers that well." TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS Stern, whose global nonprofit conducts evacuations from war zones and hostage situations, said the thwarted FlyDubai attack by "an angry, radicalized, Sunni bad guy" is showing just how far behind our enemies we are in this post-9/11 world. "They understand us significantly more than we understand them," Stern, who has been "hunting the bad guys" for 30 years, said. Stern said the U.S. has to understand the "asymmetric warfare" as well as the increasingly sophisticated enemy does. "The reason why a football coach watches game tapes is not to watch his own team play, it's to watch the bad guys play," he said. "We gotta start watching some game tapes." AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT Stern is intimately in tune with the playbook on the ground in war zones, including the Middle East and Iran. "We conduct these operations in these places still to this very day," he said. "We're actually on the ground, meaning I know people in Hezbollah, I know people in the Taliban. I know people in ISIS. I know people in ISIS-K. I've met with radical jihadi weirdos and whack jobs personally." United Arab Emirates investigators have described the incident aboard FlyDubai flight FZ1073 as an attempted terror attack after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to hijack the plane, which was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israelis. Australian authorities have also said a counterterrorism unit is investigating the co-pilot’s links to Australia. INTEL CHIEF WARNS OF 'EVOLVING' THREATS AS TERROR GROUPS NOW 'RECRUIT THEIR AGENTS ONLINE' "The bad guys are completely not afraid. They're completely emboldened. They have got the whole world to hate Israel, the whole world to hate us," he said. "It's a tough problem." Since the incident, there has been renewed vigilance in aviation and foreign airline security. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed his national security council to review security procedures for foreign civil aviation to Israel, while Vice President JD Vance said Monday that flight security procedures are also under review in the U.S. IRAN COULD MOVE SHADOW WAR IN A DANGEROUS DIRECTION, EXPERTS WARN ON BACK OF TWO POSSIBLE TERROR ATTACKS "I was asked years ago when I was still with the government," Stern said. "A team was put together and the question before the court was, if you were al-Qaeda, what would you do?" "What I came up with was ... I would get 19 hijackers, and I would hijack four airplanes, and I would fly them into buildings in America, and then issue a communique that said: 20 years of war, you are no safer today than you were before – that for TSA, and Homeland Security, and Iraq, and Afghanistan and all the different things, you are actually no safer, America, today than you were before," he said. "We're seeing, sadly," he lamented, "that academic hypothetical situation has now become a reality, or certainly a possibility." Despite President Donald Trump and the War Department's best efforts to rid the world of terrorist groups – and Iran of nuclear weapons aspirations – "you can't bomb your way into peace," Stern claimed. 'CRAZY' FLYDUBAI LANDING EXPLAINED BY ISRAELI PILOT, WHO OFFERS STEPS TO PREVENT FUTURE CRISES "They have been in holy war against us," he added. "We have now engaged in a holy war against them." "On Ramadan, the holiest month of the year in Islam, on the first day, which is the holiest day, we detonated the leader of the Shia faith, the Ayatollah," he said, likening it to "if somebody assassinated the pope on Easter Sunday while he's giving mass at the Vatican." Stern explained that rooting out ideological terror in the U.S. is more complex than ever, because even if the border is not open any longer under Trump, the terrorist networks might be infiltrating America with U.S. passport holders – making them tough to investigate, if not impossible to spot before an attack. NETANYAHU PRAISES HEROIC BYSTANDER IN BLOODY COCKPIT ATTACK FOR PREVENTING ‘ANOTHER 9/11’ Stern likened it to the release of the suspects in the RAF Fairford investigation – potential terrorist passport holders walking free. "Until I actually squeeze the triggers, I haven't committed a crime yet," he said. "Now give me an airplane." "That's the problem." Stern noted that the nature of America's adversaries in the current conflict is unlike what the U.S. faced in places like Afghanistan. "We need to remember we are very used to shooting people like the Taliban who don't know what plumbing is – who literally for years lived in caves until we showed up and gave them stuff," he continued. "The bad guys that we're talking about today are extremely sophisticated. They are extremely resourced, extremely resourceful. They're very intelligent, they're very smart, and they're very good at what they do." IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY "The Persian Empire is the only empire of empires who have been all the way on top and all the way defeated at the bottom – six times," he said. "They're looking at us going, you're 250 years old. How adorable. You're cute, America." Stern predicted that some day even 9/11 — which he survived as a first responder — is ultimately going to be dwarfed. "What will happen, probably is we'll get attacked – just like 9/11, we'll get attacked," he said. "We'll say, 'Oh my God, how did this happen?' People will wake up." "Why? Because we have created a holy war. We have now gotten into the crazy. And you cannot unring that bell."

articles.title: AP source: Trump, Rubio weigh firing U.S. envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday's Columbus Day holiday.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.

In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.

Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the U.S. embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.

After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.

The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.

A second U.S official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.

The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.

Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr.

articles.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan t...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.

"We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said.

Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.

"Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law."

Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.

"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.

"This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said.

Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices.

articles.title: Brian Fitzpatrick won by 13 points in 2024. Now, Democrats smell blood in the water.
articles.summary: An internal poll conducted by Democratic pollsters finds Fitzpatrick and challenger Bob Harvie tied among likely voters.
articles.body:
YARDLEY, Pennsylvania — Republican Brian Fitzpatrick sailed to reelection in Pennsylvania's first congressional district two years ago. But now, with just over three weeks to go until Election Day and public opinion continuing to sour on Donald Trump's presidency, Democrats smell blood in the water.

Their optimism that Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent, Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie, can defeat the five-term incumbent was on display on Saturday afternoon, as Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries and Pennsylvania's Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro hit the campaign trail in the leafy Philadelphia suburbs to drum up support for Harvie.

"A lot of people look at this race and think, 'Well, this is not really one that Democrats can win,'" Harvie told POLITICO after a rally in a middle school gym in Lower Bucks County, where supporters waved red signs emblazoned with the slogan: "Fire Fitz."

"Clearly they are wrong because Leader Jeffries thinks we can win it," Harvie said. "Governor Shapiro thinks we can win it."

Jeffries' decision to campaign alongside Harvie in the final stretch underscores Democrats' growing bullishness heading into next month's midterms, when they aim to retake control of the House of Representatives and usher in a 2018-style "blue wave."

But it also illustrates the potentially risky bets party operatives are willing to place in the final stretch of campaigning, as they deploy relatively thin resources to try and expand their electoral map, including in districts that were previously seen as out of reach.

In recent days, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has committed to spending $900,000 in its bid to unseat Fitzpatrick. House Majority PAC, the House Democrats' main super PAC, has spent more than $6 million to reserve television advertisements in the race, according to the latest AdImpact data.

"We are running through the finish line," Jeffries told reporters after Saturday's rally. "We take nothing for granted, but we are on the verge of taking back control of the House of Representatives."

Democratic operatives in the state insist Harvie is within striking distance of flipping the district, which spans all of Bucks County and a sliver of Montgomery County in the affluent Philadelphia suburbs.

A new internal poll conducted last week by Democratic pollsters Global Strategy Group found Harvie and Fitzpatrick tied, 46%-46%, among likely voters, with 8% still undecided.

In a memo first seen by POLITICO , the pollsters argued undecided swing voters would be more likely to break for Harvie in the final weeks of campaigning, noting 60% of undecideds said they would prefer Democrats take back control of Congress.

Still, Democratic leaders acknowledge that even in an increasingly favorable political environment for their party, the odds may be stacked against Harvie.

Separate internal polling commissioned by the Fitzpatrick campaign and the National Republican Congressional Committee last month showed Fitzpatrick leading Harvie by a 9-point margin. And despite the last-minute cash injection from national Democrats in the district, Fitzpatrick has long enjoyed a sizable fundraising advantage. The latest quarterly Federal Election Commission filings showed Fitzpatrick's campaign spent nearly $5 million on the race in the first six months of the year alone.

"Bob [Harvie] is running a great campaign. Brian [Fitzpatrick] is running a tough campaign," Shapiro told POLITICO at a separate stop with Democratic Party volunteers earlier on Saturday. "This is one that is going to be really close."

Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who was first elected to Congress in 2016, is widely seen as a strong candidate in Bucks County, a perennial electoral battleground at the presidential level that Shapiro has repeatedly described as the "swingiest county in the swingiest state in the whole country."

In 2024, Trump won the county over Kamala Harris by a razor-thin margin of roughly 500 votes. But the first congressional district broke narrowly for Harris, meaning the roughly 13-point win by Fitzpatrick — who has long described himself as a "fiercely independent voice" for his district — outpaced the top of the Republican ticket by double digits.

Charlie Dent, a former Republican representative from the neighboring Lehigh Valley, described Fitzpatrick as a political "unicorn," noting: "He has been able to establish a brand that is separate and independent from the president."

That puts Fitzpatrick on firmer footing than many of his Republican colleagues across the country, who are contending with an electorate that largely disapproves of Trump's leadership.

The Fitzpatrick campaign, which did not respond to POLITICO's request for an interview, has consistently emphasized the representative's bipartisan credentials, with television advertisements making little reference to the Republican Party or to Trump. The campaign and groups supporting Fitzpatrick have also run a series of negative ads attacking Harvie and accusing him of corruption. An NRCC spokesman told POLITICO Harvie had a "stagnant campaign, a significant cash disadvantage, and a disqualifying record of tax hikes and misuse of taxpayer resources." Harvie has denied any allegations of wrongdoing.

Yard signs scattered throughout the district bear slogans including "Brian Fitzpatrick For All of Us" and "Brian Fitzpatrick One Community," while campaign-sponsored billboards tout his slate of endorsements from organizations not often associated with the Republican Party, including public sector unions, animal rights and environmental groups and gun safety advocates.

"Brian is his own political force," said Christian Nascimento, a one-time Republican congressional candidate who was until earlier this year the chair of the Montgomery County Republican Committee. "I know Democrats that vote for him just because he is willing to cross the aisle and cooperate and compromise."

But Democratic leaders reject the characterization. On Saturday, Rep. Madeleine Dean, who represents Pennsylvania's fourth congressional district, said Fitzpatrick was "no moderate," calling her Republican colleague "complicit in the grotesque chaos, corruption and cruelty of this administration."

Jeffries similarly sought to tie Fitzpatrick to Trump, telling rally-goers: "A vote for the current congressman is a vote for the status quo. Bob Harvie, a vote for him is a vote to make Congress a check and balance on an out-of-control president."

Jeffries, who stands to become speaker if Democrats win the House next month, is not the only Democratic leader who has expended political capital for Harvie.

Shapiro, who is widely expected to sail to reelection next month against a relatively weak Republican opponent in state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, has also stumped alongside Harvie, as well as other congressional candidates in Pennsylvania this year. Many political operatives see Shapiro's involvement in the races as an effort to show proof of concept for his own leadership ahead of a possible presidential campaign in 2028.

"[Shapiro] identified the candidates very early on who he thought would be strongly positioned to flip these seats," Jeffries told reporters on Saturday. "Bob Harvie was among those right at the top of the list."

Asked about his involvement in congressional races on Saturday, Shapiro told POLITICO: "Success on election night isn't just about reelecting me, but making sure we are winning all the way down the ballot."

Shapiro has not said publicly whether he intends to run for the White House. In a debate against Garrity last week, Shapiro sidestepped a question about whether he would commit to serve a full four-year term in Harrisburg if reelected, saying: "The only thing I am focused on is running for re-election as governor."

A Quinnipiac University poll out last week showed Shapiro with a 25-point lead over Garrity. But asked on Saturday if Democrats risked being overconfident of their chances heading into election day, the governor responded: "I run every race like I am 25 points behind, and so I'm running taking nothing for granted."

articles.title: Prominent Republican senator says Trump's Russian diesel deal may be illegal
articles.summary: By Jan Wolfe Oct 11 (Reuters) - Republican US Senator Thom Tillis on Sunday said President Donald Trump's diesel supply ​deal with Russia may be illegal and...
articles.body:
Oct 11 (Reuters) - Republican US Senator Thom Tillis on Sunday said President Donald Trump's diesel supply deal with Russia may be illegal and will put American lives at risk, adding to bipartisan criticism of the arrangement announced by the president on Friday.

Trump ‌said that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed ‌to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.

"I do believe there's a legitimate case for saying the president's not following the law," Tillis, an influential Republican from North Carolina who ​is retiring from the Senate at the end of his term in January, told NBC's "Meet the Press" with Kristen Welker.

Prices for diesel — used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking — are near record highs and could hurt Trump's fellow Republicans in next month's congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain their thin majorities in Congress.

Analysts have said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the Trump administration ‌will follow through with the deal using existing legal ⁠authority, adding that the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down.

"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or ⁠the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told the "Fox & Friends" program.

Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican who died in July. Graham, a longtime Russia hawk, was a staunch backer of ​the ​legislation.

Tillis is not the first Republican to criticize the deal. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of ​Nebraska said on X on Friday that "propping up (Russian President Vladimir) ‌Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."

Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a "betrayal" of Graham's legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.

"The president's actions and his comments over the last 24 hours are the exact opposite of the intent of that bill," Tillis said, adding, "I will guarantee you at the first opportunity Putin has to embarrass or undermine President Trump, he will."

As Trump's poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada.

The Senate's No. ‌2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel deal on Sunday, telling CBS' "Face the ​Nation" that Trump is focused on bringing costs down for consumers, ranchers, farmers and truckers.

"The ​president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said.

Canadian Prime ​Minister Mark Carney in a call on Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy made it clear that the US-Russia diesel ‌deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and ​our allies to create peace and stability ​in Europe," his office said in a statement.

In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" that would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate.

Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details ​of the deal.

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important ‌that Russia support it as well," Zelenskiy said in a post on the Telegram app.

But there was no word from Moscow on ​the announcement, which followed days of US pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

(Reporting by Jan Wolfe and ​Ismail Shakil; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Susan Fenton, Bill Berkrot and Mark Porter)
