articles.title: AI should empower Americans. Their data shouldn’t empower China.
articles.summary: Former officials Juan Caro and Peter Brown argue that U.S. AI policy must protect Americans’ sensitive personal data from foreign adversaries like China while fostering technological innovation.
articles.body:
Somewhere in Kansas, a grandmother uses a pharmacy app to manage prescriptions, receive refill reminders, and arrange pickup. An AI assistant could make that routine easier, helping her understand instructions and prepare questions for her pharmacist.

That is technology serving a human purpose: helping someone stay independent and spend more time with the people she loves.

But she should not have to surrender her privacy to enjoy those benefits. Her health information should never become a resource for the Chinese Communist Party.

Americans use AI to write, learn, plan, and solve problems. Some embrace its possibilities; others worry about losing control over their work, choices, and information. Beneath those differences lies common ground.

People want agency: the ability to direct their own lives. They want purpose: meaningful work, stronger relationships, and time for what matters. They want security: confidence that their families and country are protected.

American AI policy should deliver all three.

AI can help entrepreneurs compete, workers develop skills, and caregivers navigate demanding days. It can expand opportunity and strengthen human judgment. Americans should be able to enjoy those advantages confidently.

But using a helpful tool is not permission to sell the details of your life to a foreign adversary.

China does not have to steal every piece of information it wants. Commercial data markets can provide another route.

In 2023, Duke University researchers purchased sensitive information about American military personnel, veterans, and their families for as little as 12 cents. Available information included health, financial, religious, and demographic details.

Those findings exposed a national security vulnerability. Records that seem mundane individually can become revealing when combined. Health information, location histories, and financial details can expose routines, relationships, and vulnerabilities.

AI makes such information easier to analyze at scale. An adversary could use it to identify military families, target government personnel, or sharpen influence operations. Information collected to make life easier could become a tool for surveillance and coercion.

Privacy and American strength therefore belong in the same conversation. Protecting personal information preserves citizens’ freedom to act while denying adversaries opportunities to exploit them.

Washington has begun addressing this threat. The Justice Department’s Data Security Program , effective since April 2025, prohibits or restricts certain transactions giving countries of concern, including China, access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and government-related data.

That foundation should be enforced and strengthened while preserving beneficial AI development.

First, give Americans meaningful control. Companies should clearly explain what sensitive information they collect, why they need it, and whether they share it. Services should collect only what they require and offer practical choices about unrelated uses. A daily prescription reminder should not require surrendering control over an intimate medical history.

Second, make national security protections follow the data. Regulators should scrutinize intermediaries, ownership, and onward transfers so adversaries cannot evade restrictions by routing purchases through another country. Enforcement should address deliberate efforts to split transactions to avoid applicable thresholds.

Third, establish workable federal standards for privacy-preserving data use. Removing names alone may not prevent identification. Standards should require testing for reidentification risk, documentation of lawful sourcing, safeguards against misuse, and accountability for subsequent transfers.

These protections would give American researchers and businesses clearer rules for developing useful AI. Privacy should be built into innovation, giving consumers confidence and companies greater certainty.

Finally, Commerce and Justice should coordinate their authorities and assess whether targeted export controls could address sensitive AI-training data transfers beyond existing protections. Additional controls should address demonstrable national security risks and provide clear compliance guidance.

Americans should not have to become data-security experts to refill a prescription or use a digital assistant. Businesses and government must make responsible choices possible and enforce protections against foreign exploitation.

Our ambition should be powerful American technology worthy of public trust. AI should help citizens make decisions, pursue meaningful work, and live securely.

The grandmother in Kansas should use her pharmacy app confidently. The entrepreneur should grow a business. The worker should master new tools.

Their information should serve their ambitions, not Beijing’s.

America will lead in AI by expanding opportunity and protecting the freedom that gives innovation its purpose. More agency. Greater purpose. Stronger security. That is an AI future Americans can share.

Juan Caro is a former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce and senior fellow for Law and Justice Policy at America First Policy Institute. Rear Admiral Peter Brown (ret.) is the former Homeland Security advisor to the president at the White House and senior fellow for Western Hemisphere Security and Maritime Affairs at America First Policy Institute.

articles.title: Daughters of the American Revolution axes chapter that challenged transgender membership
articles.summary: DAR's National Board voted to disband the Martha Laird Chapter in Texas, which led efforts to block transgender women from joining the organization.
articles.body: The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) voted Saturday to disband its Martha Laird Chapter in Texas that fought to bar transgender women from joining the historic organization, citing violations of its national bylaws. In a letter to chapter members, DAR Organizing Secretary General Marguerite Hogan Fritsch announced that the National Board of Management had approved the chapter's dissolution by a two-thirds majority vote. "On October 10, 2026, at the meeting of the National Board of Management of the National Society, Daughters of the American Revolution a resolution passed by two-thirds majority vote to disband the Martha Laird Chapter, NSDAR," Fritsch said in the letter. "The actions of the chapter have been found in violation of Article XIX, Section 4 of the Bylaws of the National Society Daughters of the American Revolution," the letter continued. The letter did not identify the specific conduct that constituted a violation or state whether the chapter's opposition to transgender membership contributed to the decision. SORORITY ALUMNAE TAKE LEGAL FIGHT TO FEDERAL COURT AFTER BEING 'GIVEN A BROTHER' INSTEAD OF SISTERHOOD The National Society Daughters of the American Revolution confirmed to Fox News Digital that the organization had voted to disband the local Texas chapter but denied it was due to its views on membership. "The National Board of Management voted on October 10 to disband the Martha Laird Chapter in Texas after finding that chapter officers had used the chapter’s name, leadership positions, communications, and governance processes to further the goals of a separate advocacy organization," the group told Fox News Digital. "The Board determined that it was this use of chapter authority and resources – not the views being advocated – that constituted conduct discrediting the National Society under Article XIX, Section 4 of the National Bylaws." "The Board’s decision was not based on the chapter’s or its members’ views concerning membership eligibility, their efforts to propose changes to the National Bylaws, or their right to advocate for changes in National Society governance," the statement continued. The group noted that at their June 2026 meeting, national members had rejected a resolution to add further membership restrictions. Individual members of the Texas chapter retain their DAR membership and are free to advocate for changes to the National Bylaws through the Society’s established governance processes, the organization said. ALL-WOMEN'S SCHOOL WELLESLEY COLLEGE RESPONDS TO ACCUSATIONS OF ADMITTING BIOLOGICAL MALE TRANS STUDENTS The chapter previously challenged DAR leadership's position on transgender membership, with member Laura McDonald telling Fox News Digital last year that the organization was contradicting its founding mission by recognizing transgender women as eligible members. "But, then they go on to say that a man who claims he's a woman is a woman, and therefore he's eligible for membership. But if you are a man that doesn't claim to be a woman, you're not eligible for membership," McDonald said. Conservative California superintendent candidate Sonja Shaw told Fox News Digital that women and girls are being told that spaces created to protect their privacy, dignity, and opportunities "no longer belong to them," including sports, restrooms, locker rooms, and now, according to her, the Daughters of the American Revolution."The women of the Martha Laird Chapter in Texas stood their ground. They sought to preserve a definition of "Daughters" based on biological sex and asked for a clear vote. On October 10, national leadership dissolved their chapter," Shaw said. SMITH COLLEGE 'MAKES A MOCKERY' OF ALL-WOMEN STATUS BY ADMITTING TRANSGENDER STUDENTS, EDUCATION WATCHDOG SAYS "Think about that. Women who stood up for their convictions saw their chapter, with a history dating back to 1942, dissolved. Here is the damning question national leadership needs to answer: Why should women be punished for standing up for the very definition of the organization they belong to?" she added. Shaw also pointed to similar debates across the country concerning sports and privacy in women's spaces, and said "this is about more than one chapter.""Our daughters deserve a future where they never have to ask permission to stand up for the truth, and where no woman is punished for having the courage to speak it," Shaw said. Under DAR's national bylaws, Article XIX, Section 4 authorizes the National Board of Management to discipline or disband chapters that violate organizational rules or engage in conduct that discredits the DAR. The dissolution comes nearly three months after Rep. Ben Cline, R-Va., introduced the Daughters of the American Revolution Membership Integrity Act, which would amend DAR's congressional charter to restrict membership to biological women. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., subsequently introduced companion legislation in the Senate. "Rather than honoring and preserving a lineage-based organization for women, it has embraced radical gender ideology at the expense of the women it was created to serve," Cline said. In September 2024, the Martha Laird Chapter, supported by 11 other chapters, submitted a proposed bylaw amendment defining membership eligibility based on biological sex. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The Center for American Liberty also provided legal assistance to the chapter, challenging DAR leadership's contention that excluding transgender applicants could jeopardize the organization's tax-exempt status. The proposed amendment was rejected by DAR's National Board of Management in February 2025. McDonald criticized the decision at the time. "The rejection by the National Board of Management of our proposal to define a woman in our bylaws sadly confirms what we knew all along – that leadership is taking a political stance which is not based on fears of the loss of 501(c)(3) nonprofit status," McDonald said in a statement to Fox News Digital. DAR, founded in 1890, previously maintained that its longstanding membership policies allowed women with legally amended birth certificates to join, provided they otherwise met the organization's genealogical requirements. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the dissolution notice, Martha Laird Chapter members will be transferred to member-at-large status and have until Nov. 9 to secure acceptance into another chapter. The letter also directed that dues previously remitted to the chapter be refunded.

articles.title: El-Sayed addresses past Obama criticism, says Democrats now ‘stand on the shoulders of giants’
articles.summary: On Sunday, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) addressed past criticism he made about former President Obama and said that he and other Democratic candidates “stand on the shoulders of giants” like the former president. “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker from NBC News asked El-Sayed about his past remarks on Obama. El-Sayed wrote in…
articles.body:
On Sunday, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) addressed past criticism he made about former President Obama and said that he and other Democratic candidates “stand on the shoulders of giants” like the former president.

“Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker from NBC News asked El-Sayed about his past remarks on Obama. El-Sayed wrote in a Huffington Post op-ed after the former president’s reelection in 2012 that “Obama was not the right choice. He just wasn’t the wrong one.” The Michigan Democrat also named off his disagreements with Obama’s record of deportations and expansion of drone warfare in the Middle East, among other criticisms.

“Well, we’ve lived through two [President] Trump terms now,” El-Sayed responded. “So, look, I know that President Obama was handed a really difficult set of circumstances, and he did his best.”

El-Sayed later said that his campaign and Democratic candidates in 2026 might “push on in different ways than his administration.”

“But it is to say that where we push differently is because we’ve learned from what he’s done and because we stand on the shoulders of giants,” the Michigan Democrat said. “And so, I am so grateful to have been a young man in my 20s with Barack Hussein Obama as president. I would never have seen myself running for office.”

El-Sayed said he could not fully express how much he appreciates the former president and described Obama as having the “elegance, the grace, the commitment under pressure” for being given “the basket of terrible things he was handed by the [former President George W.] Bush era” and that Obama “handled it all.”

“You go up and you start to appreciate just how hard change is and how important it is to pick up and push,” the candidate said.

Obama is set to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Oct. 24, the Great Lakes State’s first day of in-person early voting , nearly one month after former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned with El-Sayed. Obama will also campaign alongside Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic candidate in Michigan’s gubernatorial race.

El-Sayed said in a statement last Tuesday that he “cannot wait” for Obama to return to Michigan, calling the former president “a champion for healthcare access and a historical trailblazer of our time.”

“He knows what it means to deliver for Michiganders – that’s why he won our state twice,” El-Sayed said. “His support is critical as we fight to put Michigan families first by bringing down costs and ending Trump’s chaos in Washington.”

The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ projects a 70-percent probability of El-Sayed winning the Senate race and defeating Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), who the election handicapper gave a 30-percent probability of fending off the Democrat.

articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) slammed President Trump’s deal with Russia for diesel Sunday amid the energy struggles the U.S. is experiencing.

“The president needs to move forward with the sanctions bill that we sent him. This agreement with pursing Russian oil is essentially, I think, tarnishing [Sen.] Lindsey Graham’s [(R-S.C.)] efforts to try and get the sanctions bill through,” Tillis told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press.”

“So, the president should implement the sanctions bill, not be wide open to Russian energy,” he added.

Trump announced Friday that Russia will provide the U.S. and global market with diesel. The move comes only a few weeks out from the midterm elections, in which increasing energy prices are a central issue.

The president said Moscow will “immediately” give 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

Last month, Trump officially signed a Russia sanctions bill into law, allowing for additional sanctions and tariffs against Moscow amid its war with Ukraine.

The bill was championed by Graham, the late South Carolina senator, and pushes for Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five buyers of energy from Russia or on countries assisting Russia in avoiding sanctions.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Why North Carolina is shifting Democratic
articles.summary: Democrats have the wind at their backs in North Carolina, particularly in the race for Senate, where former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, is up against Republican political operative Michael Whatley to replace retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). Based on polling, nonpartisan ratings and campaign ​shifts, Cooper seems poised to win. A national Republican PAC…
articles.body:
Democrats have the wind at their backs in North Carolina, particularly in the race for Senate, where former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, is up against Republican political operative Michael Whatley to replace retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Based on polling, nonpartisan ratings and campaign ​shifts, Cooper seems poised to win. A national Republican PAC last week moved money out of North Carolina and into Kansas, once thought a much harder shot for Democrats. A Democratic group tied to Senate Democratic leadership also took down some ads .

It’s all a rush of indicators that Cooper and Democrats down the ballot are likely to be successful. North Carolina is seen as more and more of a swing state, although the state’s voters have swung for Republican presidents for decades with the exception of President Obama in 2008.

The Cooper campaign is taking nothing for granted.

“A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades, and North Carolina is a 50-50 state,” campaign manager Jeff Allen said. “We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense.”

The Senate stakes in particular are high, as Democrats are looking for every opportunity to flip Republican-held seats in hopes of regaining their majority. They need to take at least four seats, and that’s if they don’t lose any.

The Democrats’ success, political minds in the state say, is in large part due to Cooper, who has never lost an election and has maintained a folksy, likable and scandal-free brand.

But Tar Heel Democratic optimism goes beyond the Senate: Two House races that should be safer for Republicans, including one that was redistricted to be such, are also looking less like a GOP slam dunk. And there’s even a chance Republicans could lose their majority in the state Legislature, although that is less likely.

Chris Cooper, a professor of public policy at Western Carolina University, said the demographics of the state aren’t necessarily bluer. While there’s been an increase of younger, more liberal voters moving to North Carolina’s urban areas, it’s been balanced out by further entrenchment in the rural areas, which have become politically redder in the President Trump era. But the state still has a Democratic governor and a handful of Democratic state officials, with a Republican majority in the Legislature.

Chris Cooper, who is not related to the Senate candidate, said Democrats are also benefiting from Whatley’s status as being relatively unknown in the state compared with the four-time attorney general and two-term governor.

“We’re having this conversation less than a month until the election, and there’s already been thousands and thousands of votes cast in the state of North Carolina, and people still don’t know who the guy is,” Chris Cooper said.

Whatley was the Republican National Committee chair from 2024 to 2025 and a key figure in Trump’s second reelection contest. Before that, he was the chair of the state Republican Party for years.

But Chris Cooper said it’s difficult to beat the longtime governor’s name ID.

“His secret sauce, in some ways, is mayonnaise, right?” he said. “He’s been able to avoid scandal. He is rhetorically disciplined. You could spend all month looking for rhetorical gaffes from Roy Cooper, and you’re just not going to find any. So he’s a careful politician; he doesn’t make rhetorical mistakes; he is disciplined on the stump, and that has all amounted to a multi-decade career in North Carolina politics as a Democrat.”

The Whatley campaign and national Republicans, including Trump, have sought to dampen that reputation by pointing to Roy Cooper’s record on crime. North Carolina had, in 2024, a slightly higher homicide rate than the national average , and Cooper came under fire for releasing a batch of inmates in 2021, during the peak of the pandemic, to resolve a legal case about COVID-19 spreading within the prisons.

The GOP has run ad after ad, taking Roy Cooper to task for that move and drawing a line, sometimes inaccurately , between the inmate release and violent crimes committed in recent years.

But public safety may not be a salient enough issue for voters, according to Michael Bitzer, a professor of politics and history at Catawba College.

Bitzer mentioned a Catawba and YouGov survey conducted in September that showed voters’ primary concerns are the economy and inflation , regardless of party. Crime, while a concern, ranked below those issues and worries about protecting democracy.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee, which supports Republican candidates, went beyond Cooper’s record on crime in a statement.

“Roy Cooper drove healthcare costs to the highest the nation, put men back in women’s bathrooms, and released violent criminals from prison early,” said Nick Puglia, a spokesperson for NRSC. “Cooper’s far-left agenda is dangerous and too extreme for North Carolina.”

Now, Whatley’s campaign has no ads scheduled after this week. Bitzer said that could indicate that the campaign is rethinking the message. But time is running out to shape voters’ minds, as early voting starts Thursday.

“So I don’t think that that strategy, as long as they’ve been running it, has had the effect that they were hoping for,” Bitzer said. “And I think the real question is, you know, do they pivot to acknowledge the issue of affordability now, or do they try and position some other issue at play?”

Democrats’ optimism is also showing up in downballot races. Statehouse Republicans redrew the district map last year to make it more favorable to the GOP, but the two most competitive districts are still not guaranteed wins.

In the 1st Congressional District covering northeastern North Carolina, Rep. Don Davis (D) has managed to shift the race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” in political forecasts .

Another district, the 11th, which blankets western North Carolina, is rated as a “toss-up.” The traditionally Republican region was devastated by Hurricane Helene in 2024, and three counties in the district shifted leftward in the election a few weeks later, even as Trump won the state. Now, incumbent Rep. Chuck Edwards (R) is not running again, after allegations that he engaged in unprofessional conduct toward female staffers resulted in a censure by the House.

His replacement on the ballot, state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom (R), is lesser known than her Democratic opponent, Jamie Ager, a farmer and entrepreneur who has been campaigning for months.

Even safer Republican incumbents seem nervous: Rep. Richard Hudson (N.C.), the chair of House Republicans’ campaign arm, has reportedly reserved more than $200,000 in ad spending in his own district, which voted for Trump by 16 points in 2024.

The state does have a history of ticket-splitting, as shown by Roy Cooper’s wins in years the state went for Trump. Bitzer said he could see the potential for voters to back Cooper and then support downballot Republicans.

“I have learned over studying the state’s politics for 25-plus years never to underestimate the power of North Carolina surprising you in some way, shape or form,” Bitzer said. “So you know, will things tighten up? I think that’s everybody’s expectations. It’s going to take a lot of tightening for the Republicans to make this a close election.”

articles.title: This week on the Hill: Midterm debates, Trump Alaska trip take center stage
articles.summary: Senate and House debates return to center stage this week as candidates nationwide make their cases to voters less than a month before Election Day. The spotlight turns to contests in Iowa, Maine and New York, as both parties fight for control of Congress. President Trump, meanwhile, is set to campaign about as far from…
articles.body:
Senate and House debates return to center stage this week as candidates nationwide make their cases to voters less than a month before Election Day. The spotlight turns to contests in Iowa, Maine and New York, as both parties fight for control of Congress.

President Trump, meanwhile, is set to campaign about as far from Washington as possible. He’ll travel Tuesday to Alaska to boost Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s (R) reelection campaign. The trip follows a jaunt to Ohio on Monday.

In Iowa, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) are scheduled to face off again Tuesday, hosted by KCAU 9, as they compete for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa). Hinson has sought to publicly distance herself from Trump on certain issues, calling for an immediate end to the military conflict in Iran and arguing that Iowans are being “squeezed” at the pump.

In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins (R) and challenger Troy Jackson (D) will go head-to-head for their third and fourth debates: On Tuesday, hosted by WABI and WAGM, and Thursday, hosted by News Center Maine, Portland Press Herald and Maine Public.

Collins and Jackson already squared off twice last week, defending their records and reiterating their talking points on abortion, the economy and immigration.

In New York, WPIX-TV is also hosting a debate Thursday between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democrat Cait Conley, who are vying to represent the 17th Congressional District, which covers part of Westchester County.

Hinson and Turek to face off again: The Iowa Senate race is one of the key contests that will determine which party controls the upper chamber.

Collins and Jackson debates Nos. 3 and 4: Collins has framed herself as a moderate Republican who stands up to the Trump administration from time to time, while Jackson is a progressive Democrat.

Trump to campaign in Alaska: The president’s visit comes as the Alaska Senate race has become increasingly competitive between the incumbent and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

Lawler and Conley to spar: Lawler is trailing Conley in several polls, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated their race as a toss-up.

The debate between Hinson and Turek comes after a Friday poll from Emerson College Polling and The Hill found the Republican barely leading her Democratic opponent. Hinson notched 47 percent support, while Turek received 45 percent. Her lead is within the survey’s margin of error. Libertarian candidate Thomas Laehn received 2 percent support, and 7 percent of voters were undecided.

Hinson has publicly tried to separate herself from Trump amid voter frustrations over the rising gas and grocery costs at home. Cook Political Report refers to Iowa as “ground zero for backlash to the effect of Trump’s tariffs and Iran War on the agriculture industry.”

She has called for the House to return to session “immediately” to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax and create a diesel relief program for farmers and truckers, for instance.

During a debate between the two candidates last week, Hinson said, “I don’t want this to be a forever war, so I want to make sure we do everything we can. I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible, because I know people are getting squeezed.”

Turek, meanwhile, is running as a moderate Democrat and emphasizing his record of voting with Republicans in the statehouse. During the debate, he mentioned areas of agreement with Trump, like the prohibition of taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security and the need for a “safe and secure” southern border.

He also said he does not support Congress pursuing another impeachment of Trump, and he said lawmakers instead should focus on passing legislation to lower costs.

Collins and Jackson are slated to face off twice again this week, on Tuesday and Thursday.

Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages show Jackson, who became the party’s pick after their initial nominee withdrew this summer, leading the five-term incumbent by just over a point in the blue-leaning Pine Tree State.

The rivals clashed on the debate stage twice last week, butting heads over the military conflict in Iran, Trump’s immigration crackdown and their financial moves in the run-up to Election Day. Collins defended her decision to seek a sixth term, after pledging she would only serve for two terms 30 years ago.

Collins was reelected in 2014 by nearly 40 points, but she won her 2020 bid by a comparatively slim 9 points. She’s now considered one of the most vulnerable senators in the 2026 cycle.

At one point during the second debate last week, Jackson argued that Collins “could use her leverage to stop this war. But instead, they’re making money.”

“I mean, Senator Collins and her husband [are] making money, more, off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that’s why this doesn’t, doesn’t stop,” he said, to which Collins replied, “That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology.”

Jackson also pressed Collins on her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the nation’s highest court, tying Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision to overturn abortion rights in Roe v. Wade. Collins said she looks at justice nominees for “whether they’re fit to serve on the court” rather than trying to predict how he or she would vote on any issue.

Trump heads to Alaska for incumbent Sullivan

Trump is set to headline a midterm rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday, just one week after Vice President Vance hit the campaign trail in the state.

His visit comes as Sullivan is facing a competitive reelection bid against Peltola, as well as another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, moved the race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic” last week.

Decision Desk HQ also has Peltola slightly favored to win, while the Cook Political Report has the race listed in the “toss-up” category.

All three candidates will participate in a debate on Wednesday, hosted by AARP.

Trump has sought to boost the incumbent Alaska senator, most recently involving Dan S. Sullivan in the announcement of a $54 billion investment in a project to export natural gas from the state.

Lawler, who is fighting for his political life in a tough reelection contest, will meet Conley again on the debate stage.

The two clashed over data centers , affordability, housing and foreign policy in a debate last month. Lawler had largely touted his congressional record and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Republicans have rebranded as the Working Families Tax Cut Act, while Conley focused on what she would prioritize if elected to Congress.

Lawler also argued that he has not voted with Trump “100 percent of the time.”

What I’ve done is actually do my job, which is to represent my constituents and actually work in a bipartisan way. Why do you think Jared Golden, a Democrat from Maine, endorsed me? My best friend in Congress is Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat. We work collaboratively all the time,” Lawler said then.

A recent poll by Emerson College and PIX11 found Lawler trailing Conley, with around 48 percent of likely district voters supporting Conley, while 46 percent backed the Republican lawmaker. The remaining respondents were still undecided less than five weeks out from the November election.

Helen Huiskes, Mira Bhakta, Julia Mueller, Julia Manchester, and Sarah Davis contributed.

articles.title: Quiet part out loud: Anti-Israel mobs want one state called 'Palestine,' erasing Israel
articles.summary: Three pro-Palestinian activists tell Fox News Digital they envision replacing Israel with a single democratic state, with one proposing the name "1948."
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — This weekend, millions of anti-Israel activists marched through the streets of cities in coordinated actions from America's capital to London, Paris, Madrid and Kuala Lumpar, Malaysia, chanting the familiar refrains of "Free, free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free." But for the first time, communicated frankly in exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, three anti-Israel leaders acknowledged the goal: one state called "Palestine" encompassing modern-day Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, with a Palestinian "right of return" to the new country and equal political, voting and citizenship rights for Palestinians alongside Jews currently living in Israel. Most significantly, in the political vision they described, Israel would legally cease to exist as a separate Jewish nation-state and Jews would be quickly overwhelmed demographically. INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION' The current population of Israel is about 10 million, including about 7.8 million Jews, 2 million Palestinian Arabs (including Palestinians and most of them Muslim), and 200,000 people from other communities. There are another estimated 10.2 million Jews worldwide. There are about 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and about 8 million Palestinians in the diaspora, totaling about 13.5 million. The candor of the anti-Israel leaders lays bare the political conclusion of an argument that activists have spent years advancing on the streets, through sympathetic media outlets and in legal forums: that Israel is a "settler colonial" state practicing "apartheid" and "genocide," and therefore should not continue to exist in its current form as a Jewish state. Israeli leaders have fiercely rejected those allegations, disputing accusations of "genocide" and "apartheid" and maintaining that Israel is the nation-state of the Jewish people with equal civil and political rights for citizens that include Jews, Christians and Muslims. Advocates for Israel note that the nation's critics rarely apply the same historical lens of human-rights analysis to Arab and Muslim-majority states, many of which emerged from the collapse of empires, wars and population upheavals that displaced millions, including Jews expelled from their countries, today often restricting political, religious and minority rights. NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA In Chicago, Hatem Abudayyeh, the Palestinian-American founder of the U.S. Palestinian Community Network and a Muslim, said the new nation would be "one democratic secular state of Palestine." Jewish Israeli-born community leader Miko Peled, founder of the Palestine House in Washington, D.C., said "the proper name would be Palestine." And Maryland congressional candidate Sam Husseini, a Palestinian-American Christian, floated another name for the vision of the one state: "1948," marking the year Israel declared independence and Palestinians commemorate as the "Nakba," or catastrophe, but he said even Israeli Jews would one day accept another name: "Palestine." Their answers provide a striking interpretation from inside a movement where activists have traditionally danced around their demands with euphemisms about "liberation" and media outlets have obscured their answers even when they have been transparent. On Washington, D.C.'s First Avenue SE, Fox News Digital asked Olivia DiNucci, local coordinator for CodePink, a far-left nonprofit, what her group sees as a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In her work for CodePink, DiNucci disrupts hearings, restaurant meals and town halls to shout at lawmakers and policymakers who support the state of Israel. ‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA "Palestinians in Palestine will decide, DiNucci said. Asked if "Palestine" includes modern day Israel, she spun around and walked away. Later, she posted a message on social media, saying she was asked "gotcha questions." This weekend, protesters signaled their position with certainty, explicitly rejecting the two-state solution that has dominated international diplomacy for decades. In New York City, the Party for Socialism and Liberation circulated video of protesters marching through the streets chanting: "1-2-3-4. Occupation no more. 5-6-7-8. Israel is a terrorist state." ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS Then came the point: "We don't want no two state!" In London, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign promoted a 15-second video of a woman with a megaphone shouting: "There is only one state!" "Palestine, '48!" protesters responded. "Say it loud, say it clear!" she continued. "Palestine, you make us proud!" Back in Washington, D.C., protesters carried signs declaring, "LAND YOU HAVE 2 KILL FOR IS NOT YOURS," a message that challenged Israel's claim to the land itself, while a banner proclaiming, "THE FIGHT FOR LIBERATION IS OURS," framed the struggle as one for the territory. The demonstrators yesterday didn't address the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, but many have called them justified. ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' The one-state demand is being amplified within a powerful protest infrastructure. The broader "red-green" alliance brings socialist and communist groups together on the streets with Palestinian and Muslim activist organizations, while organizations including the Democratic Socialists of America and nonprofits in the network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon living in Shanghai, help organize, promote and amplify anti-Israel demonstrations. Singham, has poured $278 million into a pro-communist network, including CodePink, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, BreakThrough News and the ANSWER Coalition, which have become major organizing, media and logistical hubs for the protest movement. The result is a powerful infrastructure amplifying slogans such as "Free Palestine" and "from the river to the sea," even when the organizations and activists doing the amplifying don't themselves explicitly spell out the one-state political vision described to Fox News Digital. 'One democratic secular state of Palestine' From Chicago, Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Palestinian Community Network advocates for one democratic state across the territory that today encompasses Israel, the West Bank and Gaza. "Our points of unity, from the very beginning of our existence, included one democratic secular state of Palestine," he said. "And for decades and decades, we've been saying that...the only true solution that can bring peace and justice to all that live there is ... one democratic state," which includes the West Bank, Gaza and "1948 Palestinian territories," a term used to describe the land that Israel claimed as a nation in 1948. This can only happen, he said, if "the racist system of Zionism is dismantled." The ADL, a leading Jewish organization based in New York, describes Zionism as a "movement for the self-determination and statehood for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland, the land of Israel." Abudayyeh said the new state would include a "right of return" for Palestinian refugees and their descendants. "Our points of unity from day one included the right of return," he said. Activists from a U.S.-based network of groups called "Al-Awda: The Palestine Right to Return Coalition" joined the protest in Los Angeles and posted a message online: "OUR PEOPLE WILL RETURN, PALESTINE WILL BE FREE! "If all of our refugees, who have the internationally recognized right to return to Palestine, are able to return, and the system, the racist system is dismantled, then all the people there can live in peace and justice," Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital. "That's our position. It's always been our position. We're not going to abandon the five to seven million refugees that we have." "They have the right to go back to the homes and lands in which they were exiled," he explained. Abudayyeh said that wouldn't mean removing the people – most of them Jewish – living in Israel. "It doesn't mean that we're going to kick people out," he said. "It just means that these folks have an internationally recognized right, and you will never get peace and justice there unless you uphold that right." "I believe, very clearly, USPCN believes very clearly that there can be peace and justice as long as that system, that racist system of Zionism is dismantled," Abudayyeh said. "That's the essence of it." Abudayyeh compared the Palestinian movement's objective to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa. "And we're getting close to having international consensus today on the question of Israel and Zionism, where Israel doesnt have the "right to exist as a racist, Zionist, apartheid, white supremacist state." "That's what we say," he continued. "We're adamant about that. We're clear about it. Unabashed." Fox News Digital asked Abudayyeh whether "Palestine" includes modern-day Israel when protest leaders and activists chant "Palestine will be free" or "Free, free Palestine." "The majority of the majority of the people, especially in the past period, have moved to that conclusion," Abudayyeh said. 'Maybe the name of 1948' Husseini, a Palestinian-American journalist running for Congress in Maryland's 4th Congressional District, offered a similar one-state vision and an unusual proposal for what the country might be called. Standing on First Avenue SE, between the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Capitol, Husseini told Fox News Digital that his long-term vision is "one person, one vote," coupled with a Palestinian right of return. "Ultimately, long-term, I that it should be one person, one vote," Husseini said. "Why aren't they allowed back into their homes? So I think that they should," he said of Palestinian refugees. "I mean, that includes myself. I don't know that I would actually move back there, but as a descendant of a Palestinian who was forcibly displaced, I should have that right or compensation." Husseini offered another possibility for the country's name. "I've often thought of a novel proposal because people get hung up on the names. Are they going to call it Israel or are they going call it Palestine?" Husseini said. "I've toyed with the idea of calling it 1948, having a country with a number signifying the year of this cataclysm, which should be the last gasp of imperialism." If the new state is called Palestine, Husseini said, "I think a lot of Jews, when they think about it, will say, so long as they have equal rights and all are protected, will adopt the term Palestine." 'The proper name would be Palestine' Standing on Pennsylvania Avenue SE, the roar of the demonstrators getting closer as they marched from the U.S. Capitol to talks at the Palestine House of Freedom, Miko Peled, an Israeli-born Jewish activist, was equally blunt about what a "Free Palestine" means to him. "Well, our vision, our mission, and our vision is to educate people to see that a free Palestine, which means a post-Zionist, post-apartheid Palestine with equal rights and the right of the Palestinians to return, is the best vision that will benefit everybody who lives there currently, which means Israelis and Palestinians," he said. Asked whether that meant one state, he answered yes. "It's already one state, it's just an apartheid state," Peled said. "So that's our vision, to create a real democracy, free Palestine, with equal rights." Fox News Digital asked what that country would be called. "Well, historically the country was called Palestine for thousands of years and so it should be called Palestine," Peled said. "Israel is a new name. They renamed the country 78 years ago, so the proper name would be Palestine." For Peled, the familiar protest demand "Free Palestine" has a literal political meaning: One state with the new name "Palestine." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Chair of Texas Democratic Party says ‘we’re full steam ahead’ after Talarico’s flu recovery
articles.summary: The chair of the Texas Democratic Party said Sunday he is confident in Democratic senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign in the wake of his illness. “We’re full steam ahead. And, of course, you’re going to see people in the swamps of the internet making up conspiracy theories. That’s what they always do,” Kendall Scudder told…
articles.body:
The chair of the Texas Democratic Party said Sunday he is confident in Democratic senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign in the wake of his illness .

“We’re full steam ahead. And, of course, you’re going to see people in the swamps of the internet making up conspiracy theories. That’s what they always do,” Kendall Scudder told NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday.”

“But the fact of the matter is, people get sick sometimes when you’re diabetic,” he added, referencing Talarico’s Type 1 diabetes diagnosis. “It takes you a little while to get recovered.”

Talarico recently made his first public appearance in over a week after his campaign said he was recuperating from the flu. He was spotted walking around Austin City Limits (ACL), an annual music festival in the Texas city.

The Democratic Senate candidate told a reporter with The New York Times at the event on Friday he had been sick with a “nasty case of the flu” and had been “home in bed.”

Talarico’s reappearance came as his Republican opponent Ken Paxton and President Trump cast doubt on the Texas Democrat’s flu diagnosis and pushed for him to return to the campaign trail.

Texas is known to be a red state, but this year’s Senate election comes with a few asterisks.

Overall, Republicans are facing a tough electoral environment due to issues like the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s sagging approval rating and concerns about the cost of living. However, Paxton also comes with some baggage, as he faced an impeachment in the Texas House on corruption charges before he was later acquitted in the Texas Senate three years ago.

articles.title: Lawmakers in bipartisan statement push back on Trump over Russian oil
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of seven lawmakers on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee condemned President Trump’s recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which would lift sanctions on Russia and permit the flow of its oil into the global economy. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of seven lawmakers on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee condemned President Trump’s recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which would lift sanctions on Russia and permit the flow of its oil into the global economy.

“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the group wrote in a message released Sunday.

The statement is signed by three Democrats, Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Ron Wyden (Ore.), and three Republicans, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Thom Tillis (N.C.) and John Curtis (Utah).

“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute,” the bipartisan group added. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course.”

On Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social that following a conversation with Putin, Russia would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have criticized the move .

The decision followed months of increasing diesel prices , putting political pressure on the GOP as the midterms rapidly approach. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for higher costs, while some point to the war in Iran.

articles.title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as misconduct and donor bailout allegations mount
articles.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle faces mounting allegations in Greece as JD Vance and Marco Rubio weigh in on the embattled ambassador's growing controversies.
articles.body: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle may soon be fired amid reports she sought a six-figure credit card bailout from a Trump donor while offering access to administration officials, adding to mounting allegations over her conduct in Athens. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are weighing her removal, The Associated Press reported Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official. The official told the AP that a decision on what action to take would likely come this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. No departure has been confirmed. Guilfoyle, onetime fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., came under scrutiny this week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing. MARCO RUBIO ANNOUNCES SWEEPING FINANCIAL SANCTIONS AGAINST THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment. Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages. The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials. FORMER TRUMP CABINET OFFICIAL HAD 'INAPPROPRIATELY CLOSE' RELATIONSHIP WITH BODYGUARD, IG FINDS The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister has since said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made. Separately, the State Department's Office of Inspector General opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to a report from the Daily Mail. 3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claim that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos. The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported." The allegations have drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who have called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Meeks urged her removal if the allegations were substantiated. Vice President JD Vance addressed the controversy Friday, cautioning against rushing to judgment while acknowledging that misconduct should carry consequences. OHIO BAKERY WORKERS RECOUNT SURPRISE JD VANCE ENCOUNTER THAT TOOK AN UNEXPECTED TURN "Let's actually see what the facts are. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it." Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece this week and delivered remarks with the backdrop of Acropolis, declined to address the allegations directly. SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday. Rubio had defended Guilfoyle's performance a day earlier, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." FOUR AMERICAN TOURISTS AMONG 6 KILLED AFTER EXPLOSION LEVELS BUILDING NEAR ATHENS’ ACROPOLIS Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and Fox News Channel personality, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president. DONALD TRUMP JR AND BETTINA ANDERSON CELEBRATE PRIVATE WEDDING IN BAHAMAS, SHARE SWEET PERSONAL PHOTO Guilfoyle was almost Trump’s daughter-in-law. She was engaged to Don Jr. for four years, but the two publicly split in Dec. 2024 — the same month the president nominated her to be the ambassador to Greece. The president’s eldest son married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in May of this year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She was also previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, from 2001 to 2006, when he was serving as mayor of San Francisco.

articles.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.

That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.

The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.

As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.

They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".

The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.

Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.

The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.
